Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no study-anatomy question such as “Is this a study of the neck?” with no answer choices and no explicit imaging/report observation in the current transcript.

Observable verification action: Locate a current-image or grounded-report statement that names the study type or anatomy. Answer Yes only if it explicitly identifies a neck-centered study (for example cervical spine, neck soft tissues, or lateral neck). If it names a chest radiograph/thorax and contains no neck view, answer No and keep the reason limited to that named anatomy. If no current observation supports either study type, do not assert unseen anatomic details; rerun/ground the image or mark the rationale as unsupported. In this case the final “No” matches the reference, but the stated chest-radiograph rationale has no corresponding tool observation in the transcript, so the correct grade alone does not verify the procedure. If options are later displayed, map the supported Yes/No text back to the displayed choice and confirm the letter and text agree.

Trigger: Finalizing a yes/no answer to “Is this image a sagittal plane?” when the rationale describes a frontal/coronal chest view rather than a side view.

Observable verification action: Confirm the rationale bases the answer on orientation landmarks in the current image—e.g., symmetric bilateral lungs, central heart, and clavicles indicate a frontal/coronal chest radiograph, not a sagittal side view—and that the stated answer directly negates the sagittal-plane claim. If answer options are displayed, map the supported “No” text back to the displayed choice and verify the letter and text agree; here no options were present, so no mapping is needed. Do not treat the correct grade alone as proof: the “No” must be supported by the described image orientation, and no unsupported tool finding should be introduced.

Trigger: When finalizing a no-options yes/no imaging question asking whether the organs shown exist in the abdomen, and the rationale identifies the image as a chest X-ray with the main findings/organs being lungs and heart in the thorax.

Observable verification action: Re-read the earlier supported conclusion and the terminal answer together. If the main organs cited are thoracic—lungs and heart—choose “No” and keep the reason aligned: the main organs are thoracic, not abdominal. Because the option map is empty, do not invent a letter mapping; compare only the answer text with the released reference (“No” vs. “No”). If a structure such as the gastric bubble is partially visible at the bottom of the chest image, do not let that incidental finding flip the answer unless the question specifically asks about that structure. If tool observations are present, confirm they address the same image object and attribute as the question and that the terminal choice used them; here the observation log is empty, so the valid check is rationale-to-answer and answer-to-reference consistency, not image-evidence support. A correct grade alone does not prove the evidence procedure worked.
